extracted.intended_audience: speculative fiction short-story writers submitting to magazines (particularly Strange Horizons)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writers of speculative (sf/fantasy/related) short fiction about common plot types and clichés to avoid when submitting to a magazine. The page catalogs story-types the editors see too often and offers meta-advice about using the list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta: archived snapshot, not prescription
rubrics_metrics.description: This list was made by a previous editing team... Though there is some good advice here, we offer it as a curio rather than as a prescription. This is not a canonical list of bad stories or story cliches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is a snapshot of types the editors were seeing too often; it isn't complete and not everything on it is necessarily bad. It was archived to preserve links. Don't treat it as an absolute rulebook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta: don't query if your story matches list
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to query if you feel that your story might match one of the story types in this list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your story is a close match, consult well-read friends before assuming it's sufficiently different. Stories that claim to subvert the trope often turn out to be similar. Editors may not read cover letters until after the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta: don't use list as a challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: We know it's tempting to look at this list as a challenge. Please don't. In particular, please don't send us stories that intentionally incorporate one or more of these items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally writing to include these tropes will usually fail; the list is meant to discourage overused material rather than inspire pastiche submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear plot / Point A to B with no obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: Person is (metaphorically) at point A, wants to be at point B. Looks at point B, says "I want to be at point B." Walks to point B, encountering no meaningful obstacles or difficulties. The end. (A.k.a. the linear plot.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative-person-creator-block trope (generic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative person is having trouble creating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer has writer's block
rubrics_metrics.description: Writer has writer's block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painter can't paint anything good
rubrics_metrics.description: Painter can't seem to paint anything good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculptor can't sculpt anything good
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculptor can't seem to sculpt anything good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misunderstood genius creator vs critics
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative person's work is reviled by critics who don't understand how brilliant it is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muse-encounter / keeping the muse captive
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative person meets a muse (either one of the nine classical Muses or a more individual muse) and interacts with them, usually by keeping them captive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visitor ignores local rules on alien planet
rubrics_metrics.description: Visitor to alien planet ignores information about local rules, inadvertantly violates them, is punished.

rubrics_metrics.name: New diplomat ignores anthropologist's warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: New diplomat arrives on alien planet, ignores anthropologist's attempts to explain local rules, is punished.

rubrics_metrics.name: It was all a dream (twist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weird things happen, but it turns out they're not real. In the end, it turns out it was all a dream.

rubrics_metrics.name: It was all in virtual reality (twist)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the end, it turns out it was all in virtual reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist is insane / unreliable narrator twist
rubrics_metrics.description: In the end, it turns out the protagonist is insane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist writing a novel (meta-twist)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the end, it turns out the protagonist is writing a novel and the events we've seen are part of the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI loose on the Net with unclear technical grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: An AI gets loose on the Net, but the author doesn't have a clear concept of what it means for software to be "loose on the Net." (For example, the computer it was on may not be connected to the Net.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imprecise or technobabble treatment of networked systems; be clear about capabilities and infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology/modern life shown as soulless
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology and/or modern life turn out to be soulless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office-life literally or metaphorically soul-deadening
rubrics_metrics.description: Office life turns out to be soul-deadening, literally or metaphorically.

rubrics_metrics.name: All technology is soulless vs natural is good
rubrics_metrics.description: All technology is shown to be soulless; in contrast, anything "natural" is by definition good. For example, living in a weather-controlled environment is bad, because it's artificial, while dying of pneumonia is good, because it's natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utopian future is boring/perfection is bad
rubrics_metrics.description: The future is utopian and is considered by some or many to be perfect, but perfection turns out to be boring and stagnant and soul-deadening; it turns out that only through imperfection, pain, misery, and nature can life actually be good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic learning replaced by ancient book/wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: In the future, all learning is soulless and electronic, until kid is exposed to ancient wisdom in the form of a book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wise old non-electronic person redeems electronic life
rubrics_metrics.description: In the future, everything is soulless and electronic, until protagonist (usually a kid) is exposed to ancient wisdom in the form of a wise old person who's lived a non-electronic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad-person-as-protagonist (overemphasized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist is a bad person. [We don't object to this in a story; we merely object to it being the main point of the plot.]

rubrics_metrics.name: Comeuppance is actually punishment that's bad for protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad person is told they'll get the reward that they "deserve," which ends up being something bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terrorist gets comeuppance in afterlife
rubrics_metrics.description: Terrorists (especially Osama bin Laden) discover that horrible things happen to them in the afterlife (or otherwise get their comeuppance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Awful protagonist redeemed at end after long suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist is portrayed as really awful, but that portrayal is merely a setup for the ending, in which they see the error of their ways and are redeemed. (But reading about the awfulness is so awful that we never get to the end to see the redemption.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Place description with no plot or characters
rubrics_metrics.description: A place is described, with no plot or characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable 'surprise' twist ending
rubrics_metrics.description: A "surprise" twist ending occurs. [Note that we do like endings that we didn't expect, as long as they derive naturally from character action. But note, too, that we've seen a lot of twist endings, and we find most of them to be pretty predictable, even the ones not on this list.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twists should derive naturally from character action and not rely on cheap withholding of obvious information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters revealed non-human after being presented as human
rubrics_metrics.description: The characters' actions are described in a way meant to fool the reader into thinking they're humans, but in the end it turns out they're not humans, as would have been obvious to anyone looking at them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creatures revealed to be humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Creatures are described as "vermin" or "pests" or "monsters," but in the end it turns out they're humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealed obvious information revealed at end
rubrics_metrics.description: The author conceals some essential piece of information from the reader that would be obvious if the reader were present at the scene, and then suddenly reveals that information at the end of the story. [This can be done well, but rarely is.]

rubrics_metrics.name: Floating-in-void -> birth
rubrics_metrics.description: Person is floating in a formless void; in the end, they're born.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time travel used to achieve plan but plan foiled
rubrics_metrics.description: Person uses time travel to achieve some particular result, but in the end something unexpected happens that thwarts their plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-as-prankster: 'ha I tricked you' main point
rubrics_metrics.description: The main point of the story is for the author to metaphorically tell the reader, "Ha, ha, I tricked you! You thought one thing was going on, but it was really something else! You sure are dumb!"

rubrics_metrics.name: Mysteriously-named Event withheld until grim reveal
rubrics_metrics.description: A mysteriously-named Event is about to happen ("Today was the day Jimmy would have to report for The Procedure"), but the nature of the Event isn't revealed until the end of the story, when it turns out to involve death or other unpleasantness.  [Several classic sf stories use this approach, which is one reason we're tired of seeing it.  Another reason is that we can usually guess the twist well ahead of time, which makes the mysteriousness annoying.]

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit-for-ordinary-thing withheld until reveal
rubrics_metrics.description: In the future, an official government permit is required in order to do some particular ordinary thing, but the specific thing a permit is required for isn't (usually) revealed until the end of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculation-angling characters 'what if X were true' concluding implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters speculate (usually jokingly): "What if  X were true of the universe?" (For example: "What if the universe is a simulation?") At the end, something happens that implies that X is true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Far-future characters with phonetic respellings of English
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters in the story (usually in the far future and/or on an alien planet) use phrases that are phonetic respellings or variations of modern English words or phrases, such as "Hyoo Manz" or "Pleja Legions," which the reader isn't intended to notice; in the end, a surprise twist reveals that there's a connection to 20th/21st-century English speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical support call leads to wacky hijinx
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone calls technical support; wacky hijinx ensue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical support for magical/advanced items
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone calls technical support for a magical item. Someone calls technical support for a piece of advanced technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title is phone-number-style 1-800-SOMETHING-CUTE
rubrics_metrics.description: The title of the story is 1-800-SOMETHING-CUTE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientist self-experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientist uses himself or herself as test subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unethical doctor experiments on unsuspecting patient
rubrics_metrics.description: Evil unethical doctor performs medical experiments on unsuspecting patient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future criminals punished more harshly
rubrics_metrics.description: In the future, criminals are punished much more harshly than they are today.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future punishment always fits the crime
rubrics_metrics.description: In the future, the punishment always fits the crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors unaware of constitutional protections -> implausible cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The author is apparently unaware of the American constitutional amendment prohibiting cruel and unusual punishment, and so postulates that in the future, American punishment will be extra-cruel in some unusual way.

rubrics_metrics.name: White protagonist gets wise simple native advice
rubrics_metrics.description: White protagonist is given wise and mystical advice by Holy Simple Native Folk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trope often relies on reductive or stereotypical portrayals of indigenous/folk cultures; handle with nuance or avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story based on or set in D&D game/world
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is based in whole or part on a D&D game or world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party-of-D&D archetypes enter dungeon/fight monsters
rubrics_metrics.description: A party of D&D characters (usually including a fighter, a magic-user, and a thief, one of whom is a half-elf and one a dwarf) enters a dungeon (or the wilderness, or a town, or a tavern) and fights monsters (usually including orcs).

rubrics_metrics.name: D&D origin story hooking up with adventurers
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is the origin story of a D&D character, culminating in their hooking up with a party of adventurers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roleplayers transported to D&D world
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of real-world humans who like roleplaying find themselves transported to D&D world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alien/AI observes humans for comic effect but fluent in English
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien or an AI/robot/android observes and comments on the peculiar habits of humans, for allegedly comic effect. The alien or AI is fluent in English and completely familiar with various  English idioms, but is completely unfamiliar with human biology and/or with such concepts as sex or violence and/or with certain specific extremely common English words (such as "cat"). The alien or AI takes everything literally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lazy 'fish out of water' humor that depends on inconsistent worldbuilding or obvious linguistic coincidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future people comment on past oddities
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of an alien or AI, it's people in the future commenting on the ridiculous things (usually including internal combustion engines) that people used to use in the unenlightened past.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space travel solves everything / is glorious and ultimate fix
rubrics_metrics.description: Space travel is wonderful and will solve all our problems. [We agree that space travel is pretty cool, but we'd rather that weren't the whole point of the story.]

rubrics_metrics.name: Man has awful wife -> revenge vengeance
rubrics_metrics.description: Man has an awful, shrewish wife; in the end he gets revenge on her, by (for example) killing her or leaving her.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man kills 'awful' wife by accident/self-defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is entirely blameless, innocent, mild-mannered, and unobjectionable, and he kills his awful, shrewish wife entirely by accident, possibly in self-defense, so it's okay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immersive VR debate rehashed
rubrics_metrics.description: Some characters are in favor of immersive VR, while others are opposed to it because it's not natural; they spend most of the story's length rehashing common arguments on both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [Full disclosure: one of our editors once wrote a story like this. It hasn't found a publisher yet, for some reason.]

rubrics_metrics.name: Nested story: Person A tells story about Person C to Person B
rubrics_metrics.description: Person A tells a story to person B (or to a room full of people) about person C. In the end, it turns out that person B is really person C (or from the same organization). In the end, it turns out that  person A is really person C (or has the same goals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twists of identity should be handled so they don't rely on withholding trivial clues obvious to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironic but predictable twist that recasts story
rubrics_metrics.description: In the end, there's some other ironic but predictable twist that would cast the whole story in a different light if the reader hadn't guessed the ending early on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political caricature: opponents shown as stupid/evil
rubrics_metrics.description: People whose politics are different from the author's are shown to be stupid, insane, or evil, usually through satire, sarcasm, stereotyping,  and wild exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic demonization of opposing political views; nuanced portrayal is stronger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future ruled by PC liberals -> dystopia (caricature)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the future, the US or the world is ruled by politically correct liberals, leading to awful things (usually including loss of freedom of speech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Future ruled by fascist conservatives -> dystopia (caricature)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the future, the US or the world is ruled by fascist conservatives, leading to awful things (usually including loss of freedom of speech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superpowered narrator criticizes superhero genre realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Superpowered narrator claims that superhero stories never address the mundane problems that superheroes would run into in the real world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal familial sexual abuse as shock device
rubrics_metrics.description: A princess has been raped or molested by her father (or stepfather), the king.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extreme sensitivity; this is frequently used as a gratuitous plot device and can be exploitative if handled poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great breakthrough causes unforeseen world-devastating consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone comes  up with a great medical or technological breakthrough, but it turns out that it has unforeseen world-devastating consequences. [Again, this is a perfectly good plot element, but we're not thrilled when it's the whole point of the story.]

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious future character from future
rubrics_metrics.description: It's immediately obvious to the reader that a mysterious character is from the future, but the other characters  (usually including the protagonist) can't figure it out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenge-motivated protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone takes revenge for the wrongs done to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humiliation then murder
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist is put through heavy-handed humiliation after humiliation, and takes it meekly, until the end when he or she murders someone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male narrator bewildered about women (stereotyped)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator and/or male characters in the story are bewildered about women, believing them to conform to any of the standard stereotypes about women: that they're mysterious, wacky, confusing, unpredictable, changeable, temptresses, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on tired gender stereotypes as the main source of characterization or humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relentless unexplained weirdness with no payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Strange and mysterious things keep happening.  And keep happening.  And keep happening.  For over half the story.  Relentlessly.  Without even a hint of explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained surrealism needs narrative purpose or emotional payoff; otherwise readers feel strung along.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist surrounded by people who know explanation but refuse to tell
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist is surrounded by people who know the explanation but refuse to give it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is surreal dreamlike randomness
rubrics_metrics.description: Story consists mostly of surreal dreamlike randomness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrealism can work but needs coherence or thematic through-line to engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author showcases afterlife premise with little story
rubrics_metrics.description: Author showcases their premise of what the afterlife is like; there's little or no story, other than demonstrating that premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afterlife-as-business
rubrics_metrics.description: Hell and Heaven are run like businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afterlife monotonous/dull
rubrics_metrics.description: The afterlife is really monotonous and dull.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afterlife depicted as bureaucracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The afterlife is a bureaucracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afterlife is nothingness
rubrics_metrics.description: The afterlife is nothingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afterlife reunites you with loved ones (cheap comfort)
rubrics_metrics.description: The afterlife reunites you with your loved ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brutal violence against women depicted in loving detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Brutal violence against women is depicted in loving detail, often in a story that's ostensibly about violence against women being bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous or eroticized depictions of violence against women; such scenes often read exploitatively unless handled with extreme care and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man forced to rape by circumstances/magic
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is forced by circumstances or magic to rape a woman even though he really doesn't want to, honest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a problematic trope that can trivialize sexual violence; avoid using coercion-as-plot-device that excuses sexual violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female character exists chiefly to be raped
rubrics_metrics.description: The main reason for the main female character to be in the story, and to be female, is so that she can be raped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an exploitative shortcut to create drama; create fuller agency and characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evil people hook protagonist on addictive substance and ruin them
rubrics_metrics.description: Evil people hook the protagonist on an addictive substance and then start raising the price, ruining the protagonist's life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatness used as shorthand for evil/moral decay
rubrics_metrics.description: Fatness  is used as a signal of evil, dissolution, and/or moral decay, usually with the unspoken assumption that it's completely obvious that fat people are immoral and disgusting. [Note: This does not mean all fat characters in stories must be good guys. We're just tired of seeing fat used as a cheap shorthand signifier of evil.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using body size as lazy moral shorthand; if you portray fatness, do so with nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Killing target deemed okay because they're fat
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone wants to kill someone else, and that's perfectly reasonable because, after all, the victim-to-be is fat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-description of a character's fatness to signal revulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: The story spends a lot of time describing, over and over, just how fat a character is, and how awful that is. Physical contact with a fat person is understood to be obviously revolting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist goes along despite warnings, disaster follows
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist agrees to go along with a plan or action despite not having enough information about it, and despite their worries that the thing will be bad. Then the thing turns out to be bad after all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teen's family doesn't understand them
rubrics_metrics.description: Teen's family  doesn't understand them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twee fairies with wings being twee
rubrics_metrics.description: Twee little fairies with wings fly around being twee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentient toys like Toy Story interact
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentient toys, much like the ones from Toy Story, interact with each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural beings demand civil rights but face prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: In a comedic/satirical story, vampires and/or other supernatural creatures come out publicly and demand (and/or get) the vote and other rights, but people are prejudiced against them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metafictional author begins writing current story at end
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of the story,  one of the characters starts to write This Very Story that we're reading. (Often, some or all of the opening paragraph is repeated at the end.) [This is different from just ordinary first-person narration; this kind of story is usually in third person, and the Writing This Very Story is usually presented as a surprise.]

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnamed character revealed to be God
rubrics_metrics.description: An unnamed character turns out, in the end, to be God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toy/project turns out to be Earth/Universe
rubrics_metrics.description: The toy that the character is playing with (or the project that they've been working on) turns out to be Earth or the Universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story of recipes for killing/eating sentient beings
rubrics_metrics.description: Story consists of recipes for, or descriptions of, killing and eating sentient beings (usually fantastical creatures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine that prints manner of death (Machine of Death trope)
rubrics_metrics.description: There's a machine that cryptically predicts the  manner of a person's death by printing it on a slip of paper; the machine is never wrong, but often it's right in surprising or ironic ways. [There's nothing wrong with the Machine of Death anthologies, but we've seen a large number of MoD rejects, and we're extremely unlikely to buy one.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid derivative treatments of distinctive anthology premises unless you bring strong, fresh perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted modern Western power structure to sympathize with oppressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is set in a  world in which some common modern Western power structure is inverted, and we're meant to sympathize with the people who are oppressed in the world of the story. [Such stories usually end up reinforcing the real-world dominant paradigm; and regardless, they rarely do anything we haven't seen many times before.]

rubrics_metrics.name: Women have more power than men / men oppressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Women have more power than men, and it's very sad how oppressed the men are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Everyone is gay and straight people are perverts
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone in the society is gay or lesbian, and straight people are considered perverts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kids with special abilities kidnapped by government
rubrics_metrics.description: Kids with special abilities are kidnapped by the government and imprisoned and tested in a lab.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title of only digits
rubrics_metrics.description: Title consists entirely of a string of digits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child put in contrived danger to boost tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Baby or child is put in danger, in a contrived way, in order to artificially boost narrative tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using children as emotional shortcuts often reads manipulative; ensure stakes and consequences are earned and handled sensitively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magical impossible phenomenon turns out to be real (predictable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone encounters some magical or otherwise apparently impossible phenomenon. In the end, it turns out that it's real!

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrational character vindicated at end
rubrics_metrics.description: A character says things that the other characters consider to be irrational, paranoid, or obviously impossible, but in the end it turns out that character was right!

rubrics_metrics.name: Death faked as upload/transform instead of dying
rubrics_metrics.description: The author attempts to lead the reader to think a character is going to die, but instead the character is uploaded into VR or undergoes some other transformative but non-dying process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ghost wandering around learning the ropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone dies and then wanders around as a ghost. They meet other ghosts who've been around longer and who show them the ropes, and/or help them come to terms with being dead, and/or explain that nobody knows what happens after ghosts move on to the next stage of the afterlife. They're initially stuck in the place where they died or the place where their body is. In some cases, they eventually figure out how to roam the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aliens/posthumans that behave like upper-middle-class Americans
rubrics_metrics.description: Aliens and/or far-future posthumans think, talk, and behave just like upper-middle-class Americans from the 20th or early 21st century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female character lacks subjectivity; seen through male idealizing gaze
rubrics_metrics.description: The story's main (usually only) female character doesn't have much subjectivity; we see her only (or at least primarily) through the idealizing eyes of a male character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give female characters interiority and agency rather than making them props for male character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity's problems secretly caused by non-humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanity's problems (such as war, mental health issues, disease, or bad political leaders) turn out to be secretly caused by aliens, demons, or other inimical non-humans.
